Looking at this problem, I need to determine whether $\mathbb{Q}$ can be enumerated as $\{q_n\}$ so that for each positive integer $n$, only finitely many terms of the sequence lie in $A_n = \mathbb{Q} \cap [1/n, 2/n]$.

**Answer: No, it is not possible.**

**Proof:**

For each positive integer $n$, the set $A_n = \mathbb{Q} \cap [1/n, 2/n]$ is a non-degenerate interval of length $1/n > 0$, so it contains infinitely many rational numbers.

Suppose $\{q_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ is any enumeration of $\mathbb{Q}$. By definition, every rational number appears exactly once in this sequence. In particular, every element of $A_n \subseteq \mathbb{Q}$ appears as some term $q_k$. Therefore:

$$\{k \in \mathbb{N} : q_k \in A_n\} \quad\text{is in bijection with}\quad A_n$$

Since $|A_n| = \aleph_0$ (infinitely many rationals in $[1/n, 2/n]$), the set $\{k : q_k \in A_n\}$ is infinite for every positive integer $n$.

This contradicts the requirement that only finitely many elements of $\{q_n\}$ belong to $A_n$. Since the argument applies to **any** enumeration of $\mathbb{Q}$, no such enumeration exists. $\blacksquare$
